common_name: Ivory Towers Joe Pye Weed (White-Flowered Hollow Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ivory Towers is a white-flowered selection of hollow Joe Pye weed that keeps the towering scale of the species but swaps the usual mauve-pink for airy, ivory-white plumes.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where its bold late-season height won't shade out smaller neighbors. Ivory Towers produces the same huge, domed flower clusters as wild hollow Joe Pye weed, but in a cloud-like ivory white rather than the species' typical mauve-pink, giving it a lighter, more luminous presence at the back of a border or along a pond edge. Bees, butterflies, and other late-season pollinators visit the flowers just as readily as they do the straight species, and the flower heads age to a pleasant tan that holds well into winter if left standing. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom quality.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Euphoria Ruby Joe Pye Weed (Compact Early-Blooming Sweet Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Euphoria Ruby is a compact, breeder-selected sweet Joe-Pye weed bred to bloom reliably in its first season without needing the several feet of space the wild species demands.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Euphoria Ruby tolerates more average garden moisture and drier spells than full-sized Joe Pye weed once it is established, though it still performs best with regular water. This compact selection forms a tidy, upright clump topped with full-sized, vanilla-scented, dusky mauve-pink flower clusters that open earlier in summer than most Joe Pye weeds and keep coming into fall, giving pollinators an extended nectar source from a plant scaled for small borders and containers. Deer and rabbits tend to leave it alone, and it needs no staking. Cut stems back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: JoJo Joe Pye Weed (Compact Hollow Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; JoJo is a dwarf selection of hollow Joe Pye weed, reaching roughly half the height of the wild species while keeping its full-sized flower clusters.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; JoJo brings the rosy-mauve, domed flower clusters and heavy late-summer pollinator traffic of hollow Joe Pye weed down to a sturdy, self-supporting 3 to 4 foot clump that needs no staking. Its compact size makes it a much better fit than the towering species for an average perennial border, rain garden, or foundation planting near a downspout, while still drawing swallowtails, monarchs, and bees in numbers. It tolerates occasional standing water as well as normal garden moisture once established. Divide clumps in spring every few years if a larger planting is desired.

common_name: Carin Joe Pye Weed (Pale Pink Mildew-Resistant Hollow Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Carin is a European-trialed selection of hollow Joe Pye weed noted for cleaner foliage and better powdery mildew resistance than the species.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it plenty of room at the back of a border or along a pond margin where it can reach the same imposing height as the wild species. Carin was selected for excellent flower production and noticeably better resistance to powdery mildew than typical seed-grown hollow Joe Pye weed, so its coarse, lance-shaped foliage tends to stay cleaner through a humid late summer. Large, domed clusters of soft pale pink flowers open from midsummer into fall and draw heavy pollinator traffic, including migrating monarchs. Leave the sturdy stems standing through winter for structural interest and seed for songbirds, then cut back and divide congested clumps in spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Little Red Joe Pye Weed (Dwarf Sweet Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Red is a dwarf selection of sweet Joe Pye weed, reaching only a third to half the height of the wild species.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Red is a compact sweet Joe Pye weed that tolerates drier conditions than most Joe Pye selections once established, making it a practical choice for ordinary garden beds rather than only rain gardens or pond edges. It carries the same vanilla-scented foliage and domed, dusty pink-purple flower clusters as the species in miniature, staying under 4 feet and rarely needing to be staked. Late-summer blooms bring in swallowtails, monarchs, and bees at a scale that fits a small border or foundation planting. Cut stems to the ground in late winter and divide clumps every few years in spring to keep plants vigorous.

planting.note: Set out nursery divisions or container plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Mammuth is a robust, extra-tall selection of Arkansas ironweed that can reach 6 to 7 feet in a single season.

directions: Plant in full sun in average to moist, well-drained soil; Mammuth grows into a stout, self-supporting clump of narrow, willow-like leaves topped from late summer into fall by broad, flat-topped heads of intensely violet-purple flowers on stems that rarely need staking despite their imposing height. It tolerates both average garden conditions and heavier, damper soils better than many tall perennials, and its late bloom time makes it an important nectar source for bees and late-flying butterflies when many other perennials have finished. Its scale suits the back of a large border, a meadow planting, or anywhere a bold vertical accent is wanted. Cut stems back in late winter before new growth emerges and divide congested clumps in spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: White Lightning New York Ironweed (White-Flowered Ironweed)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow in fall for natural stratification; White Lightning is a true-breeding white-flowered seed strain of New York ironweed that reliably blooms from seed in its first year.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; like the wild species, White Lightning is native to wet meadows and streambanks and performs best where it never fully dries out. Unlike typical New York ironweed, its broad, flat clusters of small flowers open pure white rather than violet-purple, giving the same rigid, upright late-summer presence a brighter, more luminous look against dark-leaved companions. It flowers reliably from seed the first year and continues as a long-lived perennial, drawing bees and butterflies heavily in late summer and fall. Stake in exposed, windy sites if stems lean, and cut back in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Summer's Surrender Ironweed (Compact Mounding Hybrid Ironweed)

planting.note: Set out nursery divisions or container plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Summer's Surrender is a Chicago Botanic Garden hybrid of narrowleaf and Arkansas ironweed that forms a wide, low mound rather than an upright clump.

directions: Plant in full sun in average to moist, well-drained soil; Summer's Surrender is a bushy hybrid ironweed that inherited the fine, willowy foliage and disease resistance of narrowleaf ironweed along with the larger flowers and sturdier build of Arkansas ironweed, resulting in a wide, mounded plant that grows noticeably broader than it is tall. Its stems resist lodging even in a spot without staking, and it tolerates both average garden moisture and drier spells better than most ironweeds once established. Profuse clusters of violet-purple flowers cover the mound in August, drawing strong butterfly and bee activity late in the season. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Blind Date Boneset (Chocolate-Red Foliage Native Boneset)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Blind Date is a nativar selection of boneset bred for larger size and dark, chocolate-red new foliage that most seed-grown boneset lacks.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color develops most intensely with more direct sun, though the plant still grows and flowers well in light shade with somewhat softer color. Blind Date emerges in spring with striking chocolate-red new growth that shifts to bronze-green as the season progresses, a marked change from the plain green foliage of typical boneset, and it grows taller and more vigorously than the wild species on sturdy stems that hold up well without staking. Flat clusters of milky white flowers open in midsummer and draw heavy pollinator traffic, continuing the straight species' reputation as an excellent native nectar plant for a rain garden or pond margin. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: United States Patent and Trademark Office (Plant Patent PP35,173)
